title: How Burlesque Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of burlesque, from its 1840s-1860s British origins and the Lydia Thompson troupe and The Black Crook in America, through vaudeville, the American wheel circuits, the rise of the striptease with Gypsy Rose Lee and Sally Rand, and the Minsky brothers' legal battles, to its decline with pornography and its 1990s neo-burlesque revival. They also discuss the feminist debate over burlesque, burlesque slang, and close with listener mail about crypto-Jews and vultures at Warwick Castle.

segments.title: Opening banter and the Stripper song
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about the song 'The Stripper' by David Rose, their experiences attending burlesque shows, and the neo-burlesque revival's throwback appeal.

segments.title: Feminism debate and burlesque origins
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether neo-burlesque is pro-feminist or counter-feminist, then begin the history in 1840s-1860s Victorian Britain, where an all-female troupe lampooned society.

segments.title: Early British burlesque and The Black Crook
segments.summary: Burlesque's etymology from Italian burlesco and burla is covered, along with its satirical spoofs of the upper class. The show moved to America, where The Black Crook in 1866 drew big crowds and sparked both praise and condemnation.

segments.title: Mark Twain and Lydia Thompson's Ixion
segments.summary: Mark Twain reviewed a troupe called the Four British Blonds. Lydia Thompson then brought the first true burlesque show, Ixion, to the US, with large financial success, and American producers followed.

segments.title: Burlesque's class audience and the rise of male managers
segments.summary: Burlesque shifted from lower-class audiences to middle and upper classes in America. In the 1880s male managers took over, and strip teases gained more attention, with Little Egypt's 1893 World's Fair dance noted.

segments.title: Michael Leavitt, vaudeville format and early comics
segments.summary: Michael Leavitt's three-act format, which condensed burlesque into a single third act, is described; it influenced vaudeville. Comics such as Fanny Brice, W. C. Fields, and others began in burlesque, which was steady work.

segments.title: Burlesque wheel circuits
segments.summary: Circuits called wheels (Columbia, Empire, Mutual, and Independent) toured burlesque houses, giving performers around forty weeks of work a year for about three decades.

segments.title: Burlesque slang and the Cohen bit
segments.summary: Hosts discuss burlesque slang such as jerk, yak, skull, and mountaineer, and perform a Cohen and Cohen wordplay routine. They joke about touring.

segments.title: Striptease, the Minskys, and censorship raids
segments.summary: Talkies pushed burlesque to add more striptease, leading to its golden age. Fan dancers like Gypsy Rose Lee and Sally Rand are covered, along with police raids and the Minsky brothers' clashes with reformers and Mayor La Guardia.

segments.title: Gypsy Rose Lee, Sally Rand, and later stars
segments.summary: Gypsy Rose Lee's witty monologues combined comedy with striptease. Sally Rand's fan and bubble dances are described. Blaze Starr and Mae West are noted, and the decline of burlesque in the 1960s due to pornography is covered, followed by the 1979 Broadway show Sugar Babies.

segments.title: Neo-burlesque revival and modern performers
segments.summary: Burlesque was revived in the mid-1990s by Billy Madley in New York and Michelle Carr in Los Angeles. Modern neo-burlesque performers, including b0b, Tigger!, and Honey Wild, blend comedy, drag, and satire, and burlesque classes are described.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the burlesque discussion and sign off with a brief closing.
